summary: A small flashing light on the east side of the Pago Pago Harbor entrance, Tutuila: Navy-supervised in the 1910s, rebuilt in 1927 and run on automatic acetylene.

structures.note: Oregon pine on an angle-iron frame; in service by 1911, when the report describes it
Current post with a diamond-shaped daymark (Lighthouse Directory)

access.note: Reached by road; the entrance is unmarked. The site is open and the tower closed (Lighthouse Directory).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard Oceania District (per the Lighthouse Directory)

events.note: Last rebuilt, repaired or renovated in February 1910 (1911 inspection report)
Fourth-order lens replaced the old lens lantern; candlepower raised from 160 to 490
Reconstructed and newly equipped on 24 August 1927
Automatic acetylene lights, controlled by sun valves
A Coast Guard aids team checked the light after the earthquake and tsunami of September 2009 (photograph in the Directory)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The U.S. Lighthouse Society place record gives 'Existing: No' and 'Open to Public: No'. The Directory describes an active, maintained light, with the site open and the tower closed, and the story follows the Directory and the 1927 Bulletin. The record is not used to date anything.
The 1911 report gives the focal plane as 188 ft (57 m), the 1927 Bulletin 190 ft (58 m), and the Directory 58 m (190 ft). The figures agree within about 2 ft and are recorded as 58 m.

The 1927 Bulletin gives a white flash every five seconds; the Directory and the record give six seconds and the Directory adds 'white or red depending on direction'. No source read dates a change, so the current characteristic is recorded and the 1927 figure stays in the story.

notes_for_editor: (1) No first-lighting date is in any source read. The 1911 report says 'Prior to September 1, 1900'; the Directory says a 1907 light list omits the light. Navy-era records for 1900-1914 were not reachable. (2) Checked 2026-10-28 against the page image (PDF p. 43, printed p. 212): 'Breaker Point Light, Tutuila Island, was reconstructed and newly equipped on August 24, 1927, flashing white every 5 seconds, 190 feet high.' The 'Panama' in the OCR is a column artefact from a neighbouring list and is not used. (3) Checked 2026-10-28 against the page image: the wood-tower sentence ('towers were designed of wood, fabricated at the Tutuila Naval Station and transported knocked down') and the captain-of-the-yard sentence are as the story gives them. The Howe letter (PDF p. 19, printed p. 187) is 'received by the superintendent of lighthouses at Honolulu from Commander W. B. Howe'; it carries no date of its own, so the story does not date it. (4) The 1927 characteristic (white flash every 5 s) differs from the Directory and the record (6 s). (5) The Lighthouse Society place record says 'Existing: No'. (6) W. B. Howe is named in the 1927 letter as the retiring officer in charge of lights, American Samoa, not as a keeper of this station. He is removed from the keepers roster and appears in the story only as officer in charge. (7) The Coast Guard Historian's index lists 'Breakers Point Light (HI)'; the station is in American Samoa. (8) The Jenkins 1907 and 1922 light-list evidence is second-hand through the Directory, and the story attributes it to the Directory. (9) The NRHP nomination covers the WWII guns only and does not mention the light. (10) The 1911 report calls the site 'Private land'; current ownership is not stated in any source read. (11) The 1911 permission date '09/03/1900' is ambiguous (March 9 or September 3); not used. (12) Current lens and range are not in the sources read; the record's range (8 nm) is NOAA ENC data and is not used. (13) Checked 2026-10-28: the 1914 improvement (fourth-order lens; candlepower 160 to 490) is on PDF p. 14 under 'Improvement of light at Breaker Point, Samoa'. The Aunuu Island entry on the same page (40 to 150) is a different light and is not used. The 1915 Commissioner figures are on printed pp. 9-10 (scan pp. 15-16); the $2,100 is an approximate annual expense.
